title: Project Cybersyn
summary: Stafford Beer's team built a real-time economic feedback network for Salvador Allende's government using the Viable System Model, telex machines, and an operations room.
lesson: Cybernetic governance can move information and authority closer to where work happens. It also shows how quickly politics overtakes design.
note: Ended by the 1973 coup. Historians still debate how much it worked as intended.

sources.t: Eden Medina: Cybernetic Revolutionaries (MIT Press)

title: Risk Assessment and Horizon Scanning
summary: Singapore's government built a national horizon-scanning program informed by Cynefin and narrative sensemaking to detect weak signals early.
lesson: Sensemaking methods can be institutionalized inside a state, but they need continual protection from reverting to prediction.
note: Later commentary asks how much of the original ambition survived.

sources.t: The Cynefin Co: Horizon scanning
Integrating foresight into policy: RAHS in Singapore

title: Buurtzorg neighbourhood nursing
summary: Home care delivered by small self-managing nurse teams with minimal overhead and no middle management, scaling to thousands of nurses.
lesson: Distributed authority can scale when support functions serve teams instead of managing them.
note: Results depend on Dutch funding rules and professional nursing culture; transplants elsewhere have been mixed.

sources.t: Commonwealth Fund case study
Centre for Public Impact profile

title: Amsterdam City Doughnut
summary: The city adopted a Doughnut portrait to guide its circular economy strategy, asking how the city can thrive within planetary and social boundaries.
lesson: A shared picture of the goal can realign many departments without a single master plan.
note: Researchers question how far it has changed core economic decisions.

sources.t: DEAL: Amsterdam City Doughnut
TIME: Amsterdam is embracing a new economic theory

title: Participatory budgeting
summary: Residents deliberated and voted on a share of the city's capital budget through neighborhood and thematic assemblies, and the model spread worldwide.
lesson: Real decision power, not consultation, draws people in. Participation shifted spending toward poorer neighborhoods.
note: Weakened by later administrations; recent research documents its dismantling in its birthplace.

sources.t: WRI: Porto Alegre and the challenge of sustaining transformative change
Participedia: Porto Alegre 1989 to present
From innovation to erosion (2026)

title: Child nutrition through positive deviance
summary: Jerry and Monique Sternin worked with villages to find poor families whose children were well nourished, then helped others adopt their feeding practices.
lesson: Solutions already present in a community spread faster than imported ones, because they come from peers.

sources.t: The Vietnam story: 25 years later

title: 100,000 Lives Campaign
summary: IHI enrolled thousands of hospitals in six evidence-based changes, using improvement cycles and peer networks to spread them.
lesson: A campaign structure plus local PDSA testing can spread practice fast across independent organizations.
note: Its headline lives-saved figure was challenged by researchers, and IHI published a reply.

sources.t: IHI: 100,000 Lives Campaign ten years later
The 100,000 Lives Campaign: a scientific and policy review (PubMed)

title: Menominee Forest
summary: The Menominee Nation has managed its forest on a sustained-yield basis for generations, harvesting while the standing timber has grown.
lesson: Long-horizon stewardship rooted in relationship with land can outperform short-cycle management on both ecology and livelihood.

sources.t: Yale Environment 360: Menominee forest management
College of Menominee Nation: an Indigenous model of sustainable development (Sustainability Science, open access)

title: Student Volunteer Army
summary: After the Canterbury earthquakes, students self-organized thousands of volunteers to clear liquefaction silt, then became a lasting emergency response organization.
lesson: Spontaneous volunteers become an asset when officials make room for them and when light structure forms quickly.

sources.t: A shovel or a shopping cart: ten years of the SVA (PMC)

title: Plymouth Alliance for Complex Needs
summary: The council and health commissioners replaced competing service contracts with a single alliance of providers sharing budget and responsibility for people with complex needs.
lesson: Contract form shapes behavior. Alliance commissioning lets providers learn together instead of competing over targets.

sources.t: HLS case study: Plymouth Alliance
Co-operative Councils Innovation Network case study

title: Human Learning Systems in practice
summary: Dozens of public service organizations documenting their shift from targets and payment by results toward learning, relationships, and system stewardship.
lesson: The shift is less about a new tool than about changing funding, accountability, and management at the same time.

sources.t: HLS case studies
JRF: relational public service can tackle hardship

title: Legible Practises
summary: A free book of six stories, collected by Helsinki Design Lab, about public institutions that changed how they work and the stewardship craft behind it.
lesson: Stewardship is a craft that can be described and taught when practitioners make their decisions visible.

sources.t: Legible Practises (free book)

title: Water shortage in Ojai
summary: Carnegie Mellon's transition design team worked with residents and stakeholders to map a wicked water problem and seed interventions across timescales.
lesson: Mapping a problem with the people inside it, across long horizons, reveals where small interventions can connect.

sources.t: Words into action: transition design in Ojai (SciELO)

title: Handelsbanken and Equinor without annual budgets
summary: Two large firms dropped fixed annual budgets for rolling forecasts, relative targets, and local authority.
lesson: Budget processes are a governance structure; changing them changes what people are allowed to learn.

sources.t: Forbes: how Equinor and Handelsbanken abolished budgeting
Handelsbanken case story (Agile Business Consortium)

title: Highlander Folk School and the civil rights movement
summary: Workshops where ordinary people analyzed their own situations trained labor organizers and civil rights leaders, including Rosa Parks and Septima Clark's citizenship schools.
lesson: Popular education builds the analysis and relationships that movements later act on.

sources.t: How Myles Horton built a social movement institution
Highlander Folk School (King Institute, Stanford)

title: Haier's RenDanHeYi
summary: The appliance maker broke itself into thousands of microenterprises that contract with each other and serve users directly.
lesson: Large organizations can shrink the distance between decisions and users by dissolving middle layers.

sources.t: Corporate Rebels: RenDanHeYi

title: Wajir Peace and Development Committee
summary: After clan violence killed hundreds, women traders led by Dekha Ibrahim Abdi began mediating between clans. The agreement grew into a standing committee of elders, religious leaders, security services, officials, and NGOs.
lesson: Peace held when people from every side kept meeting to carry it out, not when a single agreement was signed. Traditional Somali ways of settling disputes did much of the work.
note: The model spread to other districts in northern Kenya; violence in the region has flared again since.

sources.t: Right Livelihood: Dekha Ibrahim Abdi (2007 laureate)
Dekha Ibrahim Abdi (Wikipedia)

title: Truth and Reconciliation Commission
summary: Public hearings across the country let victims of apartheid-era violence tell their stories and let perpetrators apply for amnesty in exchange for full disclosure.
lesson: A shared public ritual can mark a passage between two orders of society and help people move through it together.
note: Many survivors felt reparations and prosecutions never followed through; the TRC remains debated as a model.

sources.t: Truth and Reconciliation Commission (Department of Justice, South Africa)
Truth and Reconciliation Commission (Wikipedia)

title: Mont Fleur scenarios
summary: As negotiations to end apartheid began, 22 leaders from the ANC, the government, business, unions, and academia built four stories of where the country could go, named Ostrich, Lame Duck, Icarus, and Flight of the Flamingos.
lesson: Scenarios built by people who disagree can give a whole country a shared language for choices ahead, without forcing agreement on what to do.
note: Participants and facilitator Adam Kahane describe its influence; it is hard to separate from everything else happening in the transition.

sources.t: Reos Partners: Lessons from the Mont Fleur scenarios (PDF)
The Mont Fleur scenarios (Open Foresight Hub)

title: Sustainable Food Lab
summary: About 30 leaders from food companies, NGOs, and governments went on a two-year learning journey designed around Theory U, with field visits, a wilderness retreat, and prototype projects.
lesson: People who compete or oppose each other can sense a system together first and then act on what they saw, but prototypes need a home after the lab ends.
note: Became a lasting network; some prototypes stalled and the founders write openly about trial and error.

sources.t: Reos Partners: The Sustainable Food Lab, eight years and counting
Hal Hamilton: Trial and Error, a personal story (PDF)

title: People's Plan Campaign
summary: The state devolved 35 to 40 percent of its development budget to local governments. Village assemblies in every ward set priorities, and volunteers trained in large numbers helped draw up local plans.
lesson: Moving money and authority closer to people works when it comes with mass learning, so residents can actually use the power they are given.
note: Quality varied by place; later governments kept the structures but some of the campaign energy faded.

sources.t: Isaac and Franke: Local Democracy and Development (book summary)
Building local democracy: evaluating decentralization in Kerala (World Development)

title: Imagine Chicago
summary: Young people, paired with adult mentors, interviewed business, civic, and cultural leaders about what gives the city life and what they hoped for, using Appreciative Inquiry questions.
lesson: Asking what already works, and letting young people ask, can open conversations that problem-focused planning shuts down.
note: Results are mostly told as stories by the organizers; the model spread to other cities.

sources.t: Imagine Chicago: the early story
Imagine Chicago (Appreciative Inquiry Commons)

title: Government Digital Service and GOV.UK
summary: A new team in the Cabinet Office replaced hundreds of government websites with one, GOV.UK, built around user needs, user research, and small multidisciplinary teams working in the open.
lesson: Service design changes government when it comes with the authority to say no to old contracts and the skills to build in-house.
note: Its influence peaked in the early 2010s; later reviews describe a loss of central authority and uneven adoption.

sources.t: UK Government Digital Service: moving beyond a website (Harvard Kennedy School case)
The UK government's digital transformation: how did it come about? (Economics Observatory)

title: Participatory action research on Colombia's Caribbean coast
summary: Orlando Fals Borda and La Rosca worked with the national peasant users' association to research land struggles with peasants, not about them, and returned the findings in forms people could use.
lesson: Research can be a tool for the people it studies when they set the questions and own the results.
note: Historians, notably Joanne Rappaport, show how messy and contested the early practice was.

sources.t: The participatory research of Orlando Fals Borda (Participatory Methods, IDS)
Joanne Rappaport: Cowards Don't Make History (Duke University Press)

title: Deliberately developmental organizations
summary: Robert Kegan and Lisa Lahey studied companies such as Decurion that build personal growth into daily work, for example by making weaknesses and mistakes openly discussable.
lesson: Adult development can be part of how work is organized, not just a training course.
note: The evidence comes from a small number of firms studied by the theory's authors.

sources.t: Kegan, Lahey et al.: Making Business Personal (HBR, April 2014)
On deliberately developmental organizations (Harvard Graduate School of Education)

title: Embrace infant warmer
summary: Students in Stanford's Design for Extreme Affordability class were asked for a cheaper incubator. Field visits showed many babies died far from hospitals, so they designed a warmer that works without steady power.
lesson: Watching how people actually live can change the question you are answering, not just the answer.
note: Embrace later had to change its business model to reach scale; design alone did not solve distribution.

sources.t: Embrace Innovations (Wikipedia)

title: Strive Partnership
place: Cincinnati and Northern Kentucky, United States
summary: School districts, universities, funders, businesses, and nonprofits agreed on shared goals and measures for children from cradle to career, with a backbone team to coordinate them.
lesson: Organizations that each own one piece of a problem can coordinate when they share data and a common agenda.
note: The case that launched the Collective Impact model; later critiques say it underplayed community voice and power.

sources.t: Kania and Kramer: Collective Impact (SSIR, 2011)
StriveTogether: reinventing the local education ecosystem (Harvard Business School case, PDF)

title: Reframing Aging
summary: FrameWorks researched how Americans think about getting older, then worked with aging organizations to change the words and metaphors they used, such as 'older people' and 'building momentum'.
lesson: Narrative change is slow, research-led, and collective: many organizations telling a new story the same way.
note: FrameWorks links the shift to later policy, such as Colorado's 2023 Job Application Fairness Act; attribution is its own.

sources.t: FrameWorks: Impact spotlight, aging and ageism
Finding the Frame: research report (FrameWorks, 2017, PDF)

title: Artificial Anasazi
place: Long House Valley, Arizona, United States
summary: Researchers at the Santa Fe Institute and Brookings built an agent-based model of Ancestral Puebloan households from 800 to 1350 and compared it with archaeological records.
lesson: Simple rules for many varied agents can reproduce real population patterns, and show which explanations for a collapse hold up.
note: The model matched growth well but not the final abandonment, suggesting social reasons beyond the environment.

sources.t: Axtell et al.: Population growth and collapse in a multiagent model (PubMed)
Artificial Anasazi model code (CoMSES)

title: Outward Bound
summary: Shipping owner Lawrence Holt and educator Kurt Hahn started month-long courses of sailing, expeditions, and rescue training for young seamen during the Second World War.
lesson: Learning by doing hard things together, then reflecting on them, builds capacities a classroom can't.

sources.t: Outward Bound (Wikipedia)
Outward Bound USA: history

title: Women's re-entry programs study
place: New York, New Jersey, California, and Washington, United States
summary: Jack Mezirow and Victoria Marsick studied 83 women returning to college in 12 programs and found many went through a 'perspective transformation' in how they saw themselves and their roles.
lesson: Adults change most deeply when a disorienting experience meets reflection and support from others going through the same thing.
note: The founding study of transformative learning; later scholars questioned how universal its ten phases are.

sources.t: Mezirow and Marsick: Education for Perspective Transformation (Semantic Scholar)
Jack Mezirow (Wikipedia)

title: Xerox Eureka
summary: Anthropologist Julian Orr found copier technicians learned mostly by swapping stories. Xerox PARC then built Eureka, a peer-reviewed database of technicians' own repair tips, credited to their authors.
lesson: Communities of practice already exist; support works best when it amplifies how people learn from each other.
note: Widely cited in knowledge management; most accounts come from Xerox and PARC.

sources.t: Eureka! Xerox discovers way to grow community knowledge (KMWorld)
Field work in the tribal office (MIT Technology Review, 1998)

title: The New Britain workshop
summary: Kurt Lewin's team ran a workshop for community leaders on fair employment. When participants sat in on staff discussions of their own behavior, the group's here-and-now interaction became the learning.
lesson: A group studying itself as it happens can learn faster than one studying a topic.
note: Led to the National Training Laboratories at Bethel, Maine, in 1947.

sources.t: Ed Batista: A brief history of T-groups
Kurt Lewin: groups, experiential learning and action research (infed)

title: The Leicester Conference
summary: The Tavistock Institute's two-week residential conference turns the event itself into a temporary organization, so members can study authority, leadership, and group life as they happen.
lesson: Hidden group dynamics such as anxiety and projection become workable once they can be seen in the room.
note: Intense by design; some participants find it destabilizing.

sources.t: Tavistock Institute: What is a group relations conference?
Tavistock Institute: The Leicester Conference

title: Warning people 10,000 years from now
summary: The US Department of Energy's Human Interference Task Force asked how to mark nuclear waste sites so people thousands of years in the future would not dig there. Semiotician Thomas Sebeok's 1984 report, Communication Measures to Bridge Ten Millennia, treated it as a problem of signs that outlive their language.
lesson: No single sign survives that long. Sebeok recommended mixing icons, indexes and symbols, building in heavy redundancy, and relaying the message, re-encoded by each generation, rather than trusting one monument.
note: The task force's recommendations were never implemented as such. Sandia's 1993 marker study for the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant built on this work; the final marker design is still being developed.

sources.t: Science History Institute: Speaking to the future
Long Now: Communication measures to bridge 10 millennia

title: European mink on Hiiumaa and Saaremaa
summary: Semioticians at the University of Tartu studied how island communities understood the European mink, an endangered species released on Hiiumaa since 2000, to help plan a further reintroduction on Saaremaa.
lesson: An animal carries different meanings for different people. Reading those local meanings, alongside the species' own needs, reduces conflict in reintroduction.
note: A research and advisory project; the report gives recommendations rather than measured conservation outcomes.

sources.t: University of Tartu: Reintroduction of the European mink, analysis of the local community's experience
University of Tartu ecosemiotics group

title: Dialogue at a steel mill
summary: The MIT Dialogue Project, led by William Isaacs, worked with union and management at a steel mill whose relationship had been adversarial for about fifty years. They met in dialogue, with no deal on the table, to look at how they thought about each other.
lesson: Participants said they had learned to question the labels they applied to each other, and found they had more in common than they expected. Dialogue changed the relationship that later negotiations ran through.
note: Reported by the project's own lead, without independent evaluation or long-term follow-up. The source does not name the plant.

sources.t: William Isaacs: Dialogue, the power of collective thinking (The Systems Thinker)
The art of dialogue (MIT)

title: The Trojan Warrior Project
summary: A six-month US Army Special Forces experiment that taught a group of Green Berets aikido, meditation and body awareness alongside their training. Richard Strozzi-Heckler was one of the civilian teachers.
lesson: Body-based awareness can be taught as a skill inside a demanding institution, not just practised privately. It also shows how such practices get absorbed into whatever purpose the institution already has.
note: Results were mixed by the soldiers' own accounts, and no formal evaluation was published. Strozzi-Heckler's account is a first-person book.

sources.t: Richard Strozzi-Heckler (Wikipedia)
In Search of the Warrior Spirit (North Atlantic Books)

title: Despair and empowerment work after Chernobyl
summary: Joanna Macy took her workshops on despair and empowerment in the nuclear age to the former Soviet Union after the 1986 Chernobyl accident, including a 1992 workshop in Russia for people living with its effects.
lesson: Naming grief and fear together, in communities living with long-term contamination, helped turn paralysis into the energy to act and care for each other.
note: Documented mainly in tributes and practitioner accounts; there is no independent study of outcomes.

sources.t: Tricycle: Remembering Joanna Macy
Believe.Earth: Joanna Macy, pain as inspiration

title: Zero Step Warm Data Project
summary: Alongside the formal working groups of the UN High-Level Dialogue on Energy, UNDP and the International Bateson Institute co-chaired a Warm Data process, People Need People Online, to help participants see how energy access is tangled up with family, health, economy and culture.
lesson: A Warm Data process can sit beside a formal policy process without replacing it, giving people a different way to perceive the same issue.
note: The public record is an event notice; we found no published account of what changed as a result.

sources.t: UN: Zero Step Warm Data Project (side event notice)

title: Te Awa Tupua, the Whanganui River
summary: A Treaty of Waitangi settlement with Whanganui iwi recognised the river, from the mountains to the sea with its physical and metaphysical elements, as an indivisible living whole and a legal person. Two guardians, one named by iwi and one by the Crown, act as its human face.
lesson: Law can be rewritten to start from relationship: the river is treated as an ancestor and a whole, not a set of resources divided among owners.
note: Implementation is slow and contested, and legal personhood is a Western tool that only partly expresses the iwi's relationship with the river.

sources.t: Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act 2017
Whanganui District Council: Te Awa Tupua

title: Phenomenon-based learning in Finland's core curriculum
summary: Finland's national curriculum, in force from 2016, requires every school to run at least one multidisciplinary learning module each year, where pupils help plan and study a real theme across subject boundaries, alongside transversal competences.
lesson: An education system can build in time to study whole, real-world problems without abandoning subjects.
note: Early media reports that Finland had scrapped subjects were wrong; how deeply schools use the modules varies.

sources.t: Finnish National Agency for Education: New national core curriculum for basic education (PDF)
Phenomenon-based learning in Finland: a critical overview (Cogent Education, 2024)

title: Well-being of Future Generations Act
summary: Wales made long-term thinking a legal duty: public bodies must pursue seven linked well-being goals using five ways of working (long term, prevention, integration, collaboration, involvement), overseen by a Future Generations Commissioner.
lesson: Treating environmental, social and cultural crises as one pattern can be written into law, so that decisions are judged against the long term and against each other.
note: How far it changes real decisions is debated, and its duties are hard to enforce in court.

sources.t: Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 (legislation.gov.uk)
Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 (Wikipedia)

title: Chronic illness care in an Australian general practice
summary: Researchers traced how one mid-sized general practice improved its care for chronic illness over 23 years, using interviews with all staff, documents, observation and recorded practice meetings.
lesson: Care improved continuously, but not through planned system change: improvements emerged from unrelated efforts such as hiring staff for other reasons, financial pressure and technology bought for other problems. The authors found complex responsive processes described this better than planned change.
note: A single critical case, studied in depth; it shows a pattern, not a rule.

sources.t: Booth, Zwar and Harris, BMC Family Practice (2013)

title: The loss of the space shuttle Columbia
summary: Columbia broke apart on re-entry in February 2003, killing seven astronauts. Foam striking the wing at launch was the physical cause, and foam strikes had happened on earlier flights without disaster.
lesson: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board concluded that 'the NASA organizational culture had as much to do with the accident as the foam'. Known warning signs had become accepted as normal, a pattern resilience and safety science now teaches people to look for.
note: Investigations name causes after the fact; the hard part is seeing drift while it is happening.

sources.t: CAIB press release, 26 August 2003 (archived)
Congressional Research Service synopsis of the CAIB report

title: Systems thinking in Portsmouth housing repairs
summary: Portsmouth City Council's housing service, which looked after about 17,000 homes, met its targets while tenants complained about repairs. Redesigning the work around what tenants actually needed, rather than activity targets, changed the service.
lesson: Repair times fell from 24 days to 7, satisfaction rose from 60% to 99%, and the same staff completed far more jobs, according to an account citing a Wales Audit Office report. Targets had hidden the 'failure demand' created by the system itself.
note: Results come from practitioner accounts and an audit report; the approach depends on leaders willing to drop targets.

sources.t: APM: How Portsmouth Council used systems thinking (2019)
AMED: The Vanguard Method

title: The Dutch childcare benefits scandal
summary: The Dutch tax authority wrongly accused about 26,000 parents of fraud over childcare benefits. An algorithmic risk-classification system used nationality as a risk factor, and families were pushed into debt. The government resigned in January 2021.
lesson: An automated system built for efficiency amplified suspicion against people who were already marginalized, and few could appeal. The Dutch Data Protection Authority found the processing unlawful and discriminatory.
note: Algorithms were one part of a wider failure of law, politics and administration.

sources.t: Amnesty International: Xenophobic machines (October 2021)
Dutch childcare benefits scandal (overview)

title: An EU field guide for managing crises with constraints
summary: Dave Snowden and Alessandro Rancati wrote a field guide for decision makers for the European Commission's Joint Research Centre. It turns constraint thinking, which Cynefin takes from Alicia Juarrero, into practical steps for crises: set and manage boundaries, build informal structures, keep options open, distribute engagement and keep assessing the changing landscape.
lesson: The most concrete public translation of constraint-based thinking into guidance for governments that we have found so far: act on the constraints that shape what can happen, rather than issuing detailed plans.
note: Not as strong as the other cases yet. It is guidance written for decision makers, not a documented outcome; how far it has changed decisions is not yet reported, and we are watching how it plays out.

sources.t: Snowden and Rancati: Managing complexity (and chaos) in times of crisis (EU Publications Office, 2021)
Complexity Lounge #21: Alicia Juarrero, Cause and Constraints

title: A decade of research on software delivery
summary: The DORA research program, founded by Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble and Gene Kim and now part of Google Cloud, has surveyed tens of thousands of technology professionals in annual State of DevOps reports.
lesson: Fast, stable software delivery and a high-trust, generative culture go together: DORA reports that 'a high-trust, generative culture predicts software delivery and organizational performance in technology'.
note: Survey-based research; DORA itself warns against using its metrics to rank individual teams.

sources.t: DORA research program
DORA: generative organizational culture

title: The Esther network
summary: After a poor experience of one older patient, staff from Höglandet Hospital, primary care and six municipalities mapped the journey of an imagined 88-year-old, Esther, through their services and redesigned care around her. Trained 'Esther coaches' from the frontline lead improvements across organizations.
lesson: Organizing around one person's journey, with frontline coaches rather than managers driving change, can join up care across organizations that each own only part of it. Program leaders report that admissions to the hospital's medical department fell from 9,300 in 1998 to 6,500 in 2013.
note: The Commonwealth Fund notes it is difficult to attribute these changes to Esther without comparison data, and similar changes were reported elsewhere in Sweden.

sources.t: Gray, Winblad and Sarnak: Sweden's Esther Model (Commonwealth Fund, 2016, PDF)

title: Team-based car assembly at Volvo
summary: Volvo's Kalmar plant, opened in 1974, replaced the moving assembly line with about 25 teams who organized their own pace and worked on cars carried by battery-driven carriers. The later Uddevalla plant went further, with small groups building whole cars over long work cycles.
lesson: The most famous industrial test of sociotechnical design: work can be organized around autonomous teams doing whole tasks rather than fragmented line jobs.
note: Kalmar closed in 1994, and the debate continues over whether these plants could match lean production on cost or were closed for other reasons.

sources.t: Volvo Kalmar Assembly (overview)
The Volvo Uddevalla Plant and Interpretations of Industrial Design Processes (Chalmers)

title: Legislative Theatre in Rio de Janeiro
summary: As a city councillor, theatre director Augusto Boal used Theatre of the Oppressed with community groups: residents acted out problems in their lives, audiences stepped in to try alternatives, and the proposals that emerged were drafted as legislation.
lesson: Art can be a way for people to make law: Legislative Theatre turned residents' scenes into some 13 municipal laws during Boal's term, by one count.
note: Accounts differ on how many laws passed (around 13 to 15); the method depended on Boal holding office.

sources.t: Arte Útil: Theatre of the Oppressed, Legislative Theatre
Augusto Boal (overview)

title: Autism at Work at SAP
summary: The software company SAP redesigned its hiring and support so that autistic people could join its workforce, setting a goal of 1% of employees by 2020 and treating it as business strategy rather than charity.
lesson: Replacing standard interviews with other ways to assess skills, and supporting people once hired, opened access to talent that conventional processes screened out; the authors report gains in productivity, quality and innovation at companies with such programmes.
note: Reported mainly by business school case writers; the programme is a corporate initiative, and experiences of participants vary.

sources.t: Pisano and Austin: SAP SE, Autism at Work (Harvard Business School case, 2016)
Austin and Pisano: Neurodiversity as a Competitive Advantage (HBR, 2017)

title: A complexity lens on Oxfam's work in Turkana
summary: Jean Boulton studied Oxfam's programme in the Turkana region of northern Kenya through a complexity and process lens, for a chapter of Embracing Complexity: how history, context and path dependence shaped what the programme could do.
lesson: A process view asks programme designers to investigate history and what is already in motion before planning: 'History Matters', as one reviewer summed up the book's advice.
note: Not as strong as the other cases yet: the public sources describe the study but not its findings in detail, and we are watching for more documentation.

sources.t: Duncan Green, From Poverty to Power: review of Embracing Complexity (2015)
Complexity Lounge #48: Jean Boulton, Process Complexity
